problem: Disaster Recovery (Layer 5) answers a narrow question: how do we get the technical systems back online after a failure. Business Continuity asks the broader question a board member or regulator actually cares about: if this data center burns down, this key vendor collapses, or this critical employee is suddenly unreachable, does the business keep operating — payroll runs, client obligations are met, trades settle — even if imperfectly, while recovery happens in the background.

For a firm holding client funds and open trading positions, the cost of getting this wrong isn't just downtime — it can mean failing to meet a settlement obligation, being unable to answer a regulator's questions during an incident, or losing client trust at the exact moment it matters most. Business continuity turns 'we hope this never happens' into a rehearsed, funded plan.
concept: Disaster Recovery (DR) — the technical restoration of IT systems and data after an outage.

Business Continuity (BC) — the organization-wide plan for continuing critical business functions during and after a disruption, of which DR is one component alongside people, facilities, vendors, and communications.
Recovery Time Objective and Recovery Point Objective
RTO (Recovery Time Objective) — the maximum acceptable time a system or process can be down before the business impact becomes unacceptable.
RPO (Recovery Point Objective) — the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time (e.g., 'we can afford to lose the last 15 minutes of transactions, but not more').

These two numbers, set per critical business process rather than uniformly across the whole organization, drive nearly every downstream technical decision — backup frequency, replication strategy, failover architecture.

Business Impact Analysis (BIA) A BIA identifies which business functions are truly critical, ranks them by the cost of disruption over time, and is the foundational document that determines where RTO/RPO investment is justified — not every system deserves five-nines recovery; the BIA is what decides which ones do.
deep: Continuity Strategies by Tier Tier RTO Target Typical Strategy Tier 0 — Mission critical Minutes Active-active multi-region, automatic failover Tier 1 — Business critical Hours Warm standby, manual or semi- automated failover Tier 2 — Important 1-2 days Cold standby, restore from backup Tier 3 — Low priority Days to weeks Backup only, rebuild on demand People and Process Continuity Technical redundancy is only half the plan. Business continuity also requires: a defined chain of decision- making authority if key leaders are unreachable, documented procedures that don't rely on a single person's tribal knowledge, and pre-arranged communication channels that work even if primary systems (email, Slack) are the thing that's down.

Vendor and Third-Party Continuity Modern architectures depend on external vendors (cloud providers, payment processors, data feeds). A mature BC plan explicitly considers vendor failure — what happens if Supabase, Vercel, or a market-data provider has an extended outage — and whether a documented fallback or acceptable degraded mode exists.

Testing: Tabletop Exercises and Failover Drills A continuity plan that has never been tested is a hypothesis, not a plan. Tabletop exercises walk stakeholders through a simulated scenario verbally; failover drills actually execute the technical failover to validate RTO/RPO are achievable in practice, not just on paper.
workflow: A business continuity review, scaled appropriately to an internal platform or a growing side project, follows this general workflow:
1. List the critical functions this system supports (e.g., 'CEx agents submit KPIs daily,' 'clients can log into the assessment platform').
2. For each, estimate the real business cost of an hour of unavailability versus a day versus a week — this becomes the basis for an informal RTO.
3. Identify the single points of failure in the current setup — one person who knows the deployment process, one vendor with no fallback, one un-backed-up data store.
4. Write down, in plain language, what the team would actually do in the first hour of a real outage — who's notified, what the workaround is, where status is communicated.
5. Periodically re-walk this plan against what's actually changed in the system, since an outdated continuity plan can be more dangerous than none if it creates false confidence.
enterprise: Business Continuity sits at Layer 10 as the organizational capstone of everything below it — it depends on High Availability and Disaster Recovery (Layer 5) for the technical mechanics, on Reliability (Session 138) for the engineering discipline that keeps failures rare and contained, and on Security architecture (Session 140) so that a continuity event doesn't also become a security incident.

In enterprise organizations, BC is typically owned at a senior level (often reporting to COO, CISO, or a dedicated risk function) precisely because it spans technology, people, facilities, and vendor relationships — no single engineering team can own it alone.
dependencies: High Availability and Disaster Recovery (Layer 5, Sessions 79-80) — the direct technical mechanisms BC plans invoke.
Reliability (Session 138) — the engineering discipline that keeps continuity events rare in the first place.
Backup (Layer 5, Session 78) — the data-level foundation RPO targets are built on.
Monitoring and Logging (Layer 5) — the visibility needed to detect a continuity-triggering event quickly enough to act within RTO.
dependents: Compliance (Session 141) — most regulatory and framework requirements (SOC 2, financial services regulations) explicitly mandate a documented, tested BC plan.
Governance (Session 146) — the organizational oversight that keeps the BC plan current as the business and systems evolve.

Client and partner trust in a regulated firm depends directly on confidence that continuity planning exists, sometimes verified through due diligence questionnaires before a business relationship even begins.
security: A continuity event is frequently security-adjacent — ransomware is simultaneously a security incident and a business continuity event, and the response must address both simultaneously rather than sequentially.
Backup systems themselves must be secured against the same threats they're meant to recover from — backups reachable by the same compromised credentials as production are not a real recovery path.

Communication plans for a continuity event must account for the possibility that primary communication channels are themselves compromised or unavailable, requiring an out-of-band channel agreed upon in advance.

example: A prop trading firm's client-facing statement and KPI reporting depends on a single internal Google Workspace account holding all the automation scripts. If that account were suddenly locked or its owner unreachable, and no one else had documented access or admin rights, routine reporting would stop entirely — not because of any technical failure, but because of an unaddressed single point of failure in people and access, exactly the kind of gap a technical-only DR plan would miss.

A continuity-minded fix documents a secondary admin, stores critical script access/ownership information somewhere durable and reviewable, and defines who is authorized to act if the primary owner is unavailable — closing the gap without requiring any new technology, just deliberate planning.
cloud: Cloud providers' multi-region capabilities make geographically distributed continuity dramatically more accessible than in the on-premises era, but only if an organization actually architects for and tests multi-region failover rather than assuming the cloud provides it automatically.

Managed platforms (Supabase, Vercel) publish their own status pages and incident histories, which are useful inputs to a vendor dependency risk assessment — a pattern of frequent incidents on a critical vendor is a signal to plan a fallback.

For Aptimetric, a realistic vendor continuity question is: if Supabase experienced an extended outage, is there an exported, restorable copy of the question bank and user data elsewhere, or is Supabase the sole copy of record?
automation: Automated, regularly tested backups and automated failover reduce reliance on a human correctly executing a stressful manual process during an actual crisis — the same principle as automating incident response runbooks in Layer 6. Automated status monitoring that pages the right people immediately, rather than relying on someone noticing an outage, is itself a continuity control.

For a small team or solo project, the pragmatic automation equivalent is a scheduled export of critical data (e.g., a Supabase database dump, or a documented list of who has access to which Google Apps Script projects) stored somewhere independent of the primary system, so recovery doesn't depend on the primary system being the only source of truth about itself.
career: Business continuity planning experience is a strong differentiator for engineers moving toward senior infrastructure, SRE, or risk-adjacent roles, because it demonstrates the ability to think beyond 'does the code work' toward 'does the business survive if this breaks.' It's a skill regulated industries specifically screen for, given its direct tie to compliance obligations covered in the prior session.

A concrete artifact worth having — even from a personal project — is a one-page continuity plan: critical functions, RTO/RPO targets, single points of failure, and the first-hour response plan. Having written one, even informally, gives a real answer when this comes up in an interview rather than a theoretical one.

misconceptions: "Business continuity is the same thing as disaster recovery." False — DR is the technical subset;
BC also covers people, process, facilities, and vendors.
"A written plan means we're prepared." False without testing — an untested plan frequently fails in ways only a real drill reveals, such as unclear ownership or missing access.
"Every system needs the highest possible RTO/RPO." False and costly — the Business Impact Analysis exists specifically to avoid over-investing in recovery speed for low-criticality systems.

"Business continuity is only relevant to large enterprises." False — a solo project or small team has fewer redundant people and systems, arguably making basic continuity planning (documented access, off-platform backups) even more urgent, not less.
anchors: DR gets the systems back up. BC keeps the business running while that happens.
RTO = how long can we be down. RPO = how much data can we afford to lose.
An untested plan is a guess wearing a document's clothing.
connections: High Availability and Disaster Recovery (Layer 5, Sessions 79-80) — the technical mechanics BC plans sit on top of.
Reliability (Session 138) — shares the same failure-mode thinking, applied at organizational rather than purely technical scope.
Compliance (Session 141) — BC plans are frequently an explicit, auditable requirement within compliance frameworks.
Feeds directly into Governance (Session 146), where the ongoing oversight of BC plan currency and testing cadence is formalized.

lab: Hands-on exercise (conceptual — appropriately scaled to a solo/small-team context):

11. List the critical functions of the CEx Agent Platform (e.g., KPI submission, Scorecard reporting, Stellar Instant statement processing) and, separately, of Aptimetric (account access, assessment delivery, question bank integrity).
12. For each, write a one-sentence RTO ('this can be down for up to X before it's a real problem') and RPO ('we can afford to lose up to Y of data').
13. Identify the single biggest point of failure for each — a person, a vendor, an unbacked-up dataset — and write down one concrete mitigation.
14. Write the first three actions you would personally take in the first 15 minutes of discovering each system is down — this is a lightweight, personal-scale tabletop exercise.
notes: Aptimetric The most realistic continuity risk for Aptimetric right now is a Supabase-level outage or account issue, since it holds both auth and the question bank as the sole system of record. A simple, periodic export of the questions table (and eventually user data, subject to privacy considerations) to an independent location would convert an unaddressed single point of failure into a manageable one, matching the Cloud Perspective point above directly.

FundedNext CEx Agent Platform The clearest continuity gap to close is documentation of Apps Script project ownership and admin access — if the platform's automation scripts are tied to a single Google account, losing access to that account (locked, offboarded, or otherwise unavailable) would stop KPI, Scorecard, and Stellar Instant processing simultaneously. Writing down who else has or should have admin-level access, and where that information itself is stored durably (not only inside the system it describes), is the single highest-value continuity action available here without any new technical work.
